speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: asked	the Acting Minister for Education (Schools) whether the Ministry can include the topic of tripartism, in particular, the history and importance of strong tripartite relations to Singapore, in the social studies curriculum at the secondary school level.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Acting Minister for Education (Schools))
text: Through the curriculum, our student learn how positive industrial relations lead to social stability and economic growth for Singapore.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Acting Minister for Education (Schools))
text: Next, at Junior College levels, our History students study the post-Independence developmental strategies adopted by Southeast Asian countries.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Acting Minister for Education (Schools))
text: In Economics, for example, the study of policies in relation to economic restructuring, wage level management, labour productivity and mobility, allows discussion of the roles of employers, employees and government.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Acting Minister for Education (Schools))
text: More broadly, students learn about how societies build consensus because that is very important in a society, in the same way that tripartism builds consensus amongst the various stakeholders and collaboration between unions, employers and government.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Acting Minister for Education (Schools))
text: In Social Studies, our students are taught how government, the community and individuals work together for the common good of society.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Acting Minister for Education (Schools))
text: This knowledge is important because this knowledge will help our youth, especially when they eventually join the workforce, where consensus-building, mutual understanding and good relations are key.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But more than just a historical account of our tripartism journey, what we hope to impart to our youths are the values of mutual respect and understanding, of team work and collaboration, and the ability to see issues from a broader perspective.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: NTUC would be happy to work with MOE on the contents.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Please allow me to take the opportunity to reassure Members that although tripartism is not taught as a standalone topic, as I have mentioned in my response earlier, it is indeed weaved into subjects like History, Social Studies and Economics, from the lower Secondary, to the upper Secondary and even the pre-University levels.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We agree with the Member that it is not just about the historical context but consensus-building, mutual understanding, give-and-take.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: These are very important perspectives that our young should take on-board before they join the workforce.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This is why beyond teaching it from the textbook, our teachers at the pre-University level, for example, will guide these lessons and discussions to bring about the important part that tripartism plays in our economy and also society.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: In Social Studies, our teachers will facilitate discussions where differing views are respected through role playing, and then through a very experiential learning process, our students will be guided to find out how individuals and groups in the society have different needs and interests, as Mr Yong has mentioned earlier.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Our teachers then take the students through the process, so that our students can explore how government, community and individuals can work together through consensus-building and mutual understanding to contribute to the common good.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Ms Low mentioned that the history of the Labour Movement is mentioned and talked about in the Social Studies and History subjects.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: But a lot has morphed and transformed in the past decade.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: A lot of current issues and new legislations have been rolled out.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is important that the young are also acquainted with some of these new developments; not just the history but the significant and transformational development of the Labour Movement and tripartism in the past 10 years.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Many young people I engage do not know what tripartism means in our Singapore context.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Just these two points for the Parliamentary Secretary to take away.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The syllabus has to be designed to be age appropriate, so that it is pitched at a level where our students can absorb, internalise and understand.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We agree with the Member that besides the historical aspects, it is important that our students, as they move from lower Secondary, to upper Secondary, and to pre-University, can also, through the revised curriculum along the years, learn about the economic benefits of tripartism – and that definition evolves along the way – and its positive influence on the society.
